summary: When Saturn comes back to where it was at your birth, roughly every 29.5 years.
body: Astrologers treat the Saturn return as a milestone where the structures of your life — work, relationships, identity — get a hard look. The first Saturn return falls between roughly age 27 and 30; the second around age 58.

summary: The zodiac sign that was on the eastern horizon when you were born.
body: Also called the Ascendant. Many astrologers describe it as the persona — how you arrive in a room before anyone has heard you speak. Requires an accurate birth time.

summary: The highest point of the sky at the moment of birth.
body: Often abbreviated MC (Medium Coeli). Linked to vocation, public reputation, and the most visible expression of your chart. Like the rising sign, it depends on an accurate birth time.

summary: When a planet appears to move backwards from Earth's vantage point.
body: Retrograde motion is an optical effect — planets don't actually reverse — but astrologers read it as an invitation to revisit, review, or revise rather than initiate.

summary: How today's planet positions interact with your natal chart.
body: When a planet today aligns with one in your birth chart, astrologers call that a transit. Transits are why two people don't share the same daily reading even if they were born on the same day.

summary: One of 12 slices of the sky, each tied to an area of life.
body: Houses divide the chart into 12 sectors — the first house is the self, the seventh is partnerships, the tenth is career, and so on. Different house systems (Placidus, Whole-sign, Sidereal) draw the slices differently.

summary: Comparing two birth charts to see how they fit together.
body: A synastry chart overlays one person's planets on another's, looking for aspects between them. It's the technical underpinning of compatibility readings.

summary: A single chart that represents a relationship as if it were its own person.
body: Created by averaging the midpoints of two natal charts. Where synastry shows how two people interact, the composite shows the relationship itself.

summary: The most common Human Design type. About 70% of people.
body: Generators are the workhorses of the system. Their strategy is to respond — to wait for life to bring something to react to, rather than chasing.

summary: Making decisions from gut intuition, in the moment.
body: One of seven authorities in Human Design. Splenic types do best by trusting their first instinct rather than thinking it through. The signal is quiet and only speaks once.

summary: The line that curves around the base of the thumb.
body: Despite the name, palmistry doesn't read the life line as predicting how long you'll live. Most readers see it as reflecting vitality, physical resilience, and major life-shape changes.

summary: The horizontal line near the top of the palm.
body: Palmistry reads the heart line for emotional style — how you bond, how you process feelings, how you express affection.

summary: The horizontal line across the middle of the palm.
body: Read for thinking style — analytical vs intuitive, focused vs broad, decisive vs reflective.

summary: The vertical line that runs up the centre of the palm.
body: Not always visible. Palmistry reads its presence and breaks as moments where life direction shifted — career changes, relocations, identity pivots.
